The study analyzed 44 paired colorectal cancer (CRC) and normal tissue samples that produced high quality sequencing data.
miR-21 and miR-143 together comprised over 60% of the total miRNA population in the CRC samples.
In addition to miR-21 and miR-143, the study identified 8 other highly expressed miRNAs in CRC: miR-148a, -194, -192, 200b, -200c, -10b, -26a, and -145.
The researchers used a bias reduction small RNA deep sequencing protocol to profile miRNA expression in the CRC and normal tissue samples.
The bias reduction protocol allowed the researchers to obtain data from relatively large sample sizes with reduced bias in the digital miRNA profile results.
The researchers validated the dysregulation of the identified miRNAs in 10 CRC cell lines using TaqMan miRNA qPCR.
The researchers suggested that the dysregulation of the miRNAs could be caused by mutations in APC, KRAS, or TP53 in the CRC cell lines.
The researchers used the tumor-to-normal (T/N) ratio of miRNA reads and a statistical cutoff of p<0.05 to identify differentially expressed miRNAs between the CRC and normal tissue samples.

The researchers performed gene set enrichment analysis to identify oncogenic signaling pathways and biological processes that were positively or negatively correlated with the expression of miR-21, miR-200c, and miR-26a.

The researchers noted that the heterogeneity of the tissue samples and the potential for some previously reported dysregulated miRNAs to have low abundance could limit their clinical utility as biomarkers.
The researchers believe the results of this study will provide a new direction for future miRNA-related CRC development studies and the application of miRNAs in CRC diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy.
The study used a combined approach of the researchers' bias reduction small RNA deep sequencing method and the Illumina small RNA TruSeq method for sample bar coding.
The researchers obtained about 7 to 10 million small RNA reads per sample, with the majority (60-80%) being mature miRNAs.
The researchers compared their miRNA profile data with previously published CRC-miRNA results and found good agreement in the status of miRNA dysregulation.
Several previously reported dysregulated miRNAs were expressed at very low levels according to the researchers' data, suggesting they may not play a critical physiological role in CRC.
